newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia hopes for higher profile after G8 summit.
newsitem.headline: Russia hopes for higher profile after G8 summit.

text.p: Russia still hopes for a higher profile among the world's industrial powers, including full participation in crucial economic talks, a senior foreign ministry official said on Tuesday.

Vadim Lukov, head of the ministry's international policy department, told a news conference he hoped economic ties between Russia and other states would be strengthened after this month's summit of world leaders in the U.S. city of Denver.

"What is the Russian Federation's main goal as it approaches the summit? Above it is hoping for new steps in the full formation of the G8, and increasing the status of Russia in this mechanism," Lukov said.
The meeting -- grouping the leaders of the Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Japan, Italy, Russia and the United States -- will take place from June 20-22.
It is called the Summit of the Eight, but Russian President Boris Yeltsin has not yet won a seat at the Western leaders' discussions of economic issues.

"Although the mechanisms for the G8 already exist, we cannot forget that there is still the mechanism for the G7, which is the coordination of these governments' activities in world economic and credit policies," Lukov said.
"We're expecting that the Helsinki decision (to form a G8) will be strengthened."
U.S. President Bill Clinton told Yeltsin in the Finnish capital Helsinki in March that the summit would be called the "Summit of the Eight".
Japan, which has territorial disputes with Russia dating back to World War Two, had previously opposed the creation of a G8 with Russia, but it dropped its objections last month.
But Russia, still struggling to reform its ailing economy, lags far behind the other states in terms of measurements such as living standards and income per capita.

Lukov, who has helped prepare Russia's policy papers for the summit, said G8 working groups on terrorism, the environment and other problems had existed for some time, but Russia wanted to extend the cooperation into the economic field.
He expected talks to touch on efforts by indebted Russia to join the Paris Club of lender nations as a creditor and to become a full member of the World Trade Organisation.

"Our focus is now on ways to accelerate Russia's admission to the World Trade Organization, the Paris Club as a creditor nation and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development," he said.

"We believe that the depth of reform already implemented in Russia gives grounds for considering Russia a market economy...I believe the main argument the Russian side will present in Denver is a responsible and predictable policy of reform and a policy aimed at deepening economic reform in Russia.
He said talks on WTO membership would step up this year and Russia aimed to join the organisation by 1998.
A debt rescheduling agreement between Russia and the London Club of creditor banks meant that it would be easier for Russia to join the Paris Club and membership was envisaged this year.
Moscow, which inherited both the debts and the assets of the former Soviet Union, is owed large sums of money, mostly by countries in the developing world.
